Note::remove_all¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note::remove_all(std::string_view needle) const -> Note

What It Does¶

Removes every literal occurrence of a substring from each text cell.

This differs from replace in one practical way: you are not rewriting the match into something else, you are deleting it entirely.

That makes remove_all() useful for:

  • marker cleanup

  • substring erasure before tokenization

  • deleting repeated labels or prefixes without involving regex

The key behavioral point is that remove_all() is global within each cell: every matching substring is removed, not just the first occurrence and not just boundary occurrences.

Parameters¶

needle

The literal substring to remove everywhere it appears in each cell.

Interior occurrences are removed too, not just boundary occurrences. If you only want to trim a boundary run, use strip instead.

needle is treated literally. Characters such as . or * have no regex meaning here.

Returns¶

Note A shape-preserving Note with all literal occurrences removed.

Examples¶

Example 1. Remove every beta substring from each cell.

auto note = pluss::make_note({"alpha beta beta", "beta only"});
auto cleaned = note.remove_all("beta");
std::cout << "remove_all:\n" << cleaned << "\n";

Output¶

remove_all:
  [0] alpha  
  [1]  only

Example 2. Normalize the result afterward when deletion leaves boundary noise.

auto note = pluss::make_note({"##alpha##", "##beta"});
auto cleaned = note.remove_all("#");
auto normalized = cleaned.strip();
std::cout << "remove_all_strip:\n" << pluss::note::print(normalized) << "\n";

Output¶

remove_all_strip:
  [0] alpha
  [1] beta

Example 3. Remove a repeated marker substring literally. A trailing bare id remains because the pattern here is id-, not id.

auto note = pluss::make_note({"id-001-id", "id-204"});
auto cleaned = note.remove_all("id-");
pluss::tils::OutputEngine out;
out.writeln("remove_all_marker:");
out.writeln(cleaned);

Output¶

remove_all_marker:
  [0] 001-id
  [1] 204

Notes¶

  • remove_all() is literal substring erasure, not regex erasure.

  • The first example intentionally leaves doubled spaces behind. Deletion and whitespace normalization are separate concerns.

  • The third example is intentionally exact: id- is removed, but the trailing bare id in 001-id remains because it is not the same literal substring.

  • If you want the result normalized afterward, pair this with strip or another whitespace cleanup pass.

  • This is often the cleanest intermediate step before retokenizing text.

See Also¶

  • Note::replace: rewrite a substring instead of deleting it.

  • Note::strip: clean up boundary whitespace or marker runs after removal.
